practicalQuestion: Across a seven-day period containing competition, travel, limited field time, and mixed athlete availability, how should sports performance staff allocate strength, speed, conditioning, and recovery exposures while defining individual progress, hold, or adjust criteria?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with starters, non-starters, and athletes in modified participation
decisionContext.sport: Team sport with shared field and weight-room resources
decisionContext.outcome: Build a coherent plan that preserves competition readiness and appropriate chronic exposure
decisionContext.constraints: Travel; one full-team field session; varied recent minutes; no universal readiness marker; medical plans remain controlling for restricted athletes

evidenceConfidence.rationale: The pack has relevant but indirect evidence. Most of it is observational or descriptive data from male professional soccer. The sources disagree on where near-maximal speed exposure should sit relative to competition. Strength allocation, travel management, and validated readiness criteria are largely unaddressed.

dimensions.sourceReview: Two systematic reviews, two single-team descriptive or cohort studies, one large retrospective multi-team analysis, one practice-focused study, two expert or practitioner commentaries, and one case series. Several are legacy records without full-text library review.
dimensions.directness: Partial. The sources address timing of high-speed and peak-demand exposure, starter and non-starter workload gaps, and congestion. None tests a full plan for allocating strength, speed, conditioning and recovery across a week with travel and one team field session.
dimensions.consistency: Mixed. A retrospective analysis links near-maximal speed at D-2 with no match hamstring injuries. A descriptive team study found MD-2 had the least high-speed stimulus, and a practice-focused study reports that methodologies differ on MD-2.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. The populations are elite or professional male soccer players, one NFL-based practitioner article, and one collegiate football case series. There are no collegiate team-sport speed-timing data, no female athletes, and no data on athletes in modified participation.

bottomLine.text: The evidence supports planning near-maximal speed and peak-demand exposure deliberately, and adjusting it by each athlete's recent minutes. It does not agree on whether speed belongs two days before competition or mid-week. It offers little on strength allocation, travel, or a single readiness marker. Treat any progress, hold, or adjust criteria as local professional rules, not evidence-validated thresholds.

actions.title: Option A: near-maximal speed two days out
actions.text: One option is to place a near-maximal speed exposure two days before competition for athletes who will play. In elite soccer this timing was associated with no match hamstring injuries, but the data only included players who played the match. The authors say other days then need tailoring around it.

actions.title: Option B: speed and peak demands mid-week
actions.text: Another option is to concentrate high-speed and peak-demand work in the central days, away from both competitions, and keep two days out light. This matches observed professional practice, and one cohort suggests peak-demand drills on MD-4 may help prepare for match demands. With only one full-team field session, staff will need to decide which option that session serves.

actions.title: Split exposures by recent minutes
actions.text: Starters and non-starters can accumulate very different weekly loads. A practice-focused source recommends that players with limited match participation get high-speed work to narrow that gap. The evidence does not test how to deliver this outside a team field session. Group-based top-up work is a professional judgment.

actions.title: Write criteria as local rules
actions.text: Define progress, hold, or adjust rules that combine several inputs rather than one number. Sources state there is no magic number and that chronic speed dose is likely population specific. A commentary suggests deciding rotation criteria before matches. The evidence does not test any specific criterion. Thresholds you set are professional caution.

monitoring.label: Near-maximal speed exposure
monitoring.text: Record whether and on which day each athlete reached near-maximal speed in the turnaround. In elite soccer the timing of these exposures was associated with match hamstring injury occurrence.

monitoring.label: Minutes and load gap
monitoring.text: Track competition minutes and weekly load for starters versus non-starters. This shows who needs top-up exposure and who needs recovery.

monitoring.label: Training peaks versus competition
monitoring.text: Compare training peak demands with competition peak demands. In one professional cohort, training peaks did not meet match demands.

guardrails.text: Medical plans remain controlling for restricted athletes. Progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians. One collegiate football case series describes an athlete restricted to upper body lifting only. The evidence does not test how to shift exposures for restricted athletes. Avoid compensating with unplanned overload in the unrestricted body region.
Do not use any single ratio, marker, or score as an automatic progress or clearance rule. The pack does not validate one.

Congested schedules were usually linked with higher match injury incidence in professional male soccer, even though total match distance was unchanged. Stable running output should not be read as full recovery.

limitations.text: Most evidence comes from elite or professional male soccer. One source is an NFL-based practitioner article and one is a collegiate football case series. Transfer to a mixed collegiate roster is uncertain.
The designs are retrospective, descriptive, or practice reports. They show patterns and associations, not proof that one weekly schedule works better.
The commentary states there is no research-based evidence to manage travel fatigue in athletes. Travel adjustments are professional judgment.
The only weight-room evidence is a single-team case series. The pack does not address how to allocate strength exposures within a competition week.

whatCouldChange.text: Prospective or controlled comparisons of near-maximal speed at two days out versus mid-week in collegiate team-sport athletes could resolve the timing tension.
Collegiate data on top-up work for non-starters and on exposure plans for athletes in modified participation could support specific criteria.
Research-based evidence on managing travel fatigue would allow travel to be built into the plan with evidence rather than caution.

evidenceTension.text: A retrospective multi-team analysis found no match hamstring injuries when near-maximal speed exposures occurred two days before the match. A descriptive single-team study found that day had the least high-speed stimulus. A practice-focused study reports some methodologies prioritize speed on that day while others use recovery and tapering. Context does not resolve which approach fits this roster.

assumptions: The seven-day period contains one competition, so D-2 and MD-2 mean two days before that competition.
Staff have some external load tracking, such as GPS, to record speed exposure and minutes.
Restricted athletes' activity limits are set by the treating clinicians and are not changed by this brief.
coverageGaps: No source tests how to allocate strength training exposures within a competition-to-competition week.
No source provides research-based guidance for managing travel within the microcycle.
No collegiate or female team-sport data on timing of near-maximal speed or peak-demand exposure.
No validated progress, hold, or adjust criteria or universal readiness marker.
No evidence on exposure planning for athletes in modified participation. Available ACL reconditioning and return-to-play sources had no usable excerpts for this context.
Possible leads without accessible text: libraryId 617 (acute:chronic workload ratio systematic review) and libraryId 579 (Delphi consensus on sleep and jet lag).
